# Why `plt.style.use('seaborn-colorblind')` works but `plt.style.library['seaborn-colorblind']` raises KeyError

## Mechanism responsible

`matplotlib.style.core` defines a `fix_style()` helper that translates old,
deprecated `seaborn-*` style names (e.g. `seaborn-colorblind`) to their
renamed `seaborn-v0_8-*` equivalents (e.g. `seaborn-v0_8-colorblind`),
emitting a `MatplotlibDeprecationWarning` in the process. `style.use()`
calls `fix_style()` on every style name it's given before doing the actual
dictionary lookup in `library`, so `use('seaborn-colorblind')` transparently
resolves to `library['seaborn-v0_8-colorblind']` and works, warning included.

However, the module-level `library` dict itself (built by `update_user_library()`
/ `reload_library()`) is populated only with keys under the *new*
`seaborn-v0_8-*` names — the old `seaborn-*` aliases were never inserted into
it. `fix_style()` is only invoked inside `use()`; nothing applies the same
translation when code accesses `library` directly (e.g.
`plt.style.library['seaborn-colorblind']`, or iterating/looking up
`available`/`library` by hand). Since `library` is a plain `dict`, indexing
it with the old name simply falls through to a normal dict lookup and raises
a plain `KeyError`, with no deprecation warning and no redirection.

## What's wrong

The deprecated-name translation logic lives only on the `use()` code path
(`fix_style()`), not on the `library` mapping itself. This means the two
public entry points into the style subsystem — calling `use()` versus
indexing `library` — behave inconsistently for the same deprecated name:
one silently (with a warning) succeeds, the other blows up with a bare
`KeyError`. The root problem is that `library` is an ordinary `dict`, so it
has no way to intercept lookups and apply the same alias-fixing/warning
behavior that `use()` performs before hitting the dict.

## Fix

Make `library`'s lookup behavior match `use()`'s by giving it the same
alias-resolution logic, rather than duplicating/relying on translation only
inside `use()`. Concretely:

- Introduce a small `dict` subclass, e.g. `_StyleLibrary(dict)`, that
  overrides `__getitem__` (and ideally `__contains__`/`get`) to first run
  the key through the same `fix_style()` translation (issuing the same
  deprecation warning) and then fall back to normal `dict.__getitem__`
  lookup with the (possibly translated) key.
- Have `library` be constructed as an instance of `_StyleLibrary` instead of
  a plain `dict` (i.e. change `reload_library()`/module init to build
  `library = _StyleLibrary()` and populate it as before).
- Keep `use()` calling `fix_style()` as it does now (or simply have it rely
  on the now-consistent `library[name]` lookup), so both access paths funnel
  through one shared translation implementation instead of two divergent
  ones.

This way, `plt.style.library['seaborn-colorblind']` and
`plt.style.use('seaborn-colorblind')` both resolve the deprecated name to
`seaborn-v0_8-colorblind`, both emit the same deprecation warning, and
neither raises a spurious `KeyError`.

**only inside** `matplotlib.style.core.use()`, in its local nested helper
function `fix_style()` (see `lib/matplotlib/style/core.py`):

```python
def fix_style(s):
    if isinstance(s, str):
        s = style_alias.get(s, s)
        if s in [
            "seaborn",
            "seaborn-bright",
            "seaborn-colorblind",
            ...
        ]:
            _api.warn_deprecated(...)
            s = s.replace("seaborn", "seaborn-v0_8")
    return s

for style in map(fix_style, styles):
    ...
    elif style in library:
        _apply_style(library[style])
```

`use()` maps every requested style name through `fix_style`, which rewrites
`"seaborn-colorblind"` to `"seaborn-v0_8-colorblind"` (emitting the
deprecation warning) *before* looking it up in `library`. Because the actual
style sheet shipped with Matplotlib is named `seaborn-v0_8-colorblind.mplstyle`
(the old `seaborn-colorblind.mplstyle` file no longer exists /
was renamed as part of the 3.6 deprecation), only the rewritten name exists as
a key in `style.library`/`style.available`.

The bug is that this renaming/aliasing behavior is private to `use()` — it is
never applied to the `library` dict itself (nor to `available`). `library` is
built directly from the on-disk `.mplstyle` files in `read_style_directory()`
and `reload_library()`, and it only ever contains the *new* `seaborn-v0_8-*`
keys. There is no compatibility shim registered in `library`, so:

* `plt.style.use('seaborn-colorblind')` — goes through `fix_style`, gets
  translated to `'seaborn-v0_8-colorblind'`, which *is* present in `library`,
  so it works (with the deprecation warning).
* `plt.style.library['seaborn-colorblind']` — bypasses `use()`/`fix_style`
  entirely and indexes the dict directly with the old name, which was never
  inserted into `library`, hence `KeyError`.

So the inconsistency is caused by putting the deprecation-alias translation
logic in only one of the two public access paths (`use()`) instead of at the
data-structure level (`library`/`available`), even though both paths are
documented/expected to accept the same style names.

## Fix

Make `library` (and `available`) itself aware of the deprecated aliases,
instead of hard-coding the alias table only inside `use()`. Concretely:

1. Extract the `seaborn` alias list/table (currently the literal list inside
   `fix_style`) into a module-level constant, e.g. `_DEPRECATED_SEABORN_STYLES
   = {"seaborn": "seaborn-v0_8", "seaborn-bright": "seaborn-v0_8-bright", ...}`.
2. In `reload_library()` (which builds the global `library` dict), after
   populating it with the real `seaborn-v0_8-*` entries, also insert lazy /
   deprecated aliases for the old names, e.g. via a custom `RcParams`/dict
   subclass or simply:
   ```python
   for old, new in _DEPRECATED_SEABORN_STYLES.items():
       if new in library:
           library[old] = library[new]
   ```
   (or better, use a `__getitem__` override on a small "DeprecatedLibrary"
   wrapper class that emits the deprecation warning lazily when the old key is
   actually accessed, so warnings still fire on direct `library[...]` access
   too, not just through `use()`).
3. Have `use()`'s `fix_style()` simply consult this same alias table (or drop
   its special-casing altogether and rely on `library` already containing the
   old keys), so there is a single source of truth for the mapping instead of
   duplicated/inconsistent logic between `use()` and `library`.
4. Update `available` to include the deprecated names too (`sorted(library.keys())`
   already does this automatically once `library` contains them).

This way, both `plt.style.use('seaborn-colorblind')` and
`plt.style.library['seaborn-colorblind']` consult the exact same mapping and
produce consistent behavior (and consistent deprecation warnings), eliminating
the divergence between the two access paths.

  `seaborn-colorblind.mplstyle` etc. to `seaborn-v0_8-colorblind.mplstyle`

  named `seaborn-colorblind.mplstyle` any more (only
  `seaborn-v0_8-colorblind.mplstyle`), `style.library` never contains the key
  `'seaborn-colorblind'` — only `'seaborn-v0_8-colorblind'`.

  `s.replace("seaborn", "seaborn-v0_8")` before ever consulting `library`.
  Only *after* this rewriting does `use()` check `elif style in library:` and
  apply `library[style]`.

(`seaborn-v0_8-...`) happens as a private, one-off side effect inside `use()`
only. Nothing updates or aliases `style.library` (or `style.available`) with
the old names, so any other consumer of the dictionary — such as directly
indexing `plt.style.library['seaborn-colorblind']`, or iterating
`plt.style.available` looking for the old name — fails with a `KeyError`,
even though `use()` with that exact same string succeeds a line earlier.

of being expressed as data available to the `style.library` mapping itself.**
`use()` silently maps old name -> new name and then looks the new name up in

bypasses it entirely.

being buried in `use()`'s local closure. Concretely:

   ```python

       "seaborn": "seaborn-v0_8",
       "seaborn-bright": "seaborn-v0_8-bright",
       ...
   ```

2. In `reload_library()` (or right after building `library`), add these
   deprecated keys into the `library` dict too, mapping each old name to the
   same rc-param dict as its `seaborn-v0_8-*` counterpart (and likewise add
   them to `available`), for example:

   ```python

       global library
       library = update_user_library(_base_library)
       for old, new in _DEPRECATED_SEABORN_STYLES.items():
           if new in library:
   ```

   deprecation warning lazily on `__getitem__`/`__contains__` for the old

The fix is to hoist the alias mapping into shared module-level data used consistently by use(), library, and available (e.g. by also inserting alias entries into library or making library alias-aware) instead of duplicating/hiding the logic only inside use().

# Why `plt.style.use('seaborn-colorblind')` works but `plt.style.library['seaborn-colorblind']` raises KeyError

## Root cause

The alias-rewriting logic for the deprecated bare `seaborn-*` style names
(`seaborn`, `seaborn-colorblind`, `seaborn-darkgrid`, etc. → the actually
shipped `seaborn-v0_8-*` files) lives **only inside `matplotlib.style.core.use()`**,
in its local nested helper function `fix_style()`:

```python
def fix_style(s):
    if isinstance(s, str):
        s = style_alias.get(s, s)
        if s in [
            "seaborn",
            "seaborn-bright",
            "seaborn-colorblind",
            ...
        ]:
            _api.warn_deprecated(...)
            s = s.replace("seaborn", "seaborn-v0_8")
    return s

for style in map(fix_style, styles):
    ...
```

`use()` runs every requested style name through `fix_style`, which rewrites
`"seaborn-colorblind"` to `"seaborn-v0_8-colorblind"` (issuing the
deprecation warning) *before* it ever looks the name up in
`matplotlib.style.library`. Since `"seaborn-v0_8-colorblind"` really is a key
in `library` (it is one of the actual `.mplstyle` files shipped in
`lib/matplotlib/mpl-data/stylelib`), `use()` succeeds.

`matplotlib.style.library`, however, is just a plain `dict` (built once at
import time by `read_style_directory`/`update_user_library` and exposed via
module-level `__getattr__`/`_api.caching_module_getattr` machinery — see
`core.py`, bottom of the file, and `available = list(library)`). It contains
only the *real* file-derived keys such as `"seaborn-v0_8-colorblind"`, `"seaborn-v0_8"`,
etc. There is no entry, and no alias mapping, for the legacy bare names like
`"seaborn-colorblind"`. Nothing ever inserts those aliases into `library`
itself — the alias substitution table (`style_alias` dict plus the
`if s in [...]: s = s.replace(...)` block) is private, local state that only
`use()` consults.

So the inconsistency is caused by **the alias/rename translation for the
deprecated seaborn style names being implemented as one-off string
rewriting inside `use()`, rather than as data recorded in (or reachable
from) `style.library`/`style.available`.** `use()` transparently redirects
old names to new files, while direct dictionary access (`library[...]`)
bypasses that redirection entirely and only sees the "real" keys.

(This is exactly the situation that also makes `plt.style.available`
*not* contain `"seaborn-colorblind"` even though `plt.style.use` accepts it.)

## Fix

Make the alias table a first-class, shared piece of data rather than logic
buried in `use()`'s local closure, and use it consistently everywhere style
names are resolved/listed:

1. Hoist `style_alias` and the list of deprecated seaborn names (and the
   `s.replace("seaborn", "seaborn-v0_8")` rule) out of `use()` into a
   module-level mapping, e.g.

   ```python
   STYLE_ALIASES = {
       'mpl20': 'default',
       'mpl15': 'classic',
       **{name: name.replace('seaborn', 'seaborn-v0_8')
          for name in [
              'seaborn', 'seaborn-bright', 'seaborn-colorblind', ...
          ]},
   }
   ```

2. Have `use()` call a shared `fix_style()`/resolution helper that consults
   this module-level table (so behavior doesn't change for `use()`, warning
   still emitted for the deprecated names).

3. Either
   - (a) populate `library` with entries for the deprecated aliases too
     (pointing at the same rc dict as their `seaborn-v0_8-*` counterpart),
     so `library['seaborn-colorblind']` and `'seaborn-colorblind' in
     library`/`available` work and are consistent with `use()`; or
   - (b) make `library` (or provide a new accessor) alias-aware, e.g. give
     `library` a `__missing__`/subclass or wrap it so that
     `library[name]` and `name in library` first check `STYLE_ALIASES` and
     redirect (still emitting the deprecation warning) before raising
     `KeyError`.

   Option (a) is simplest and matches what actually happens in current
   matplotlib upstream: the "seaborn" aliases were kept in `library`/
   `available` (with the deprecation warning triggered lazily) so that both
   `style.use()` and direct `style.library[...]` / `style.available` behave
   the same way, instead of the alias handling being private to `use()`.

The key point of the fix is: **the alias-to-real-name mapping must be a
single, shared piece of data used by every access path (`use`, `library`,
`available`), not duplicated/hidden logic inside only one of them.**

The fix is to replace pairwise merging with a single dependency graph built from all source lists at once (edges for each adjacent pair in each list) and use a stable topological sort, only warning on genuine cycles.

# Media merge order conflict

## Responsible function
`django.forms.widgets.Media.merge` (a `@staticmethod`), invoked pairwise from
`Media.__add__` every time two `Media` objects are combined (e.g. once per
widget as `BoundField`/`Form.media` accumulates JS/CSS lists).

## What is wrong
`Media.merge(list_1, list_2)` only ever merges **two** lists at a time. It
walks `list_2` in reverse and inserts each item into a *running* copy of
`list_1` based on relative index comparisons, warning on
`MediaOrderConflictWarning` if it thinks two items are out of order.

When a form has 3+ widgets, `Form.media` builds up the combined list by
calling this two-list `merge()` repeatedly:

```
combined = widget1.media + widget2.media + widget3.media
         = merge(merge(widget1_js, widget2_js), widget3_js)
```

The problem is that after the first `merge()` call, the resulting
`combined_list` is just a flat list — it has **lost all information about
which relative orderings came from which original source list**. It is
purely positional. When the third list is then merged against this already
merged list, `merge()` can no longer tell the difference between:

- an ordering constraint that was actually stated by one of the original
  lists, and
- an accidental/incidental ordering that is merely an artifact of how the
  previous pairwise merge happened to interleave two unrelated lists.

Concretely, with:
```
ColorPicker:      ['color-picker.js']
SimpleTextWidget: ['text-editor.js']
FancyTextWidget:  ['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js']
```
`merge(color-picker, text-editor)` first produces something like
`['text-editor.js', 'color-picker.js']` (or some order), and then merging
that flat 2-item list against FancyTextWidget's list makes `merge()`
compare index positions of `text-editor-extras.js` against `color-picker.js`
and `text-editor.js` using data that no longer distinguishes "explicitly
constrained by FancyTextWidget" from "incidentally placed there by an
unrelated earlier merge". This causes it to (a) raise a bogus
`MediaOrderConflictWarning` about `text-editor.js`/`text-editor-extras.js`,
which were never in conflicting order in any single input list, and (b)
produce a final order that actually violates FancyTextWidget's own required
order (`text-editor.js` → `text-editor-extras.js` → `color-picker.js`).

In short: **pairwise/incremental merging of media lists is fundamentally
lossy** — it collapses multiple independent ordering constraints into a
single list too early, so later merges can misattribute or lose ordering
information, both producing false-positive conflict warnings and incorrect
final ordering.

## Fix
Stop merging two-at-a-time. Instead, collect **all** the media lists that
need to be combined (from every widget/subform contributing to `Form.media`)
and build one dependency graph from all of them simultaneously:

- For each individual source list, add a directed edge `a -> b` for every
  adjacent pair `a, b` in that list (meaning "a must come before b").
- Merge these edges from every list into a single graph (accumulating them
  in one dict-of-sets keyed by node, preserving insertion order for
  determinism), rather than accumulating them through a chain of pairwise
  list merges.
- Run a stable topological sort over that graph (Django added
  `django.utils.topological_sort.stable_topological_sort` for this) to
  produce the final combined order.
- Only raise `MediaOrderConflictWarning` if the topological sort detects an
  actual cycle in the graph — i.e., a genuine contradiction between two
  source lists — rather than an artifact of a two-list-at-a-time merge.

This way every ordering constraint is considered against every other
constraint from the *original* lists at once, so unrelated pairs (like
`text-editor.js`/`text-editor-extras.js` vs. `color-picker.js`, which
FancyTextWidget explicitly orders and no other widget contradicts) are never
misreported as conflicting, and the final order always respects every real
constraint (e.g. FancyTextWidget's `text-editor.js, text-editor-extras.js,
color-picker.js`).

results.finishSummary: Media.merge() in django/forms/widgets.py merges JS lists pairwise, losing track of which ordering came from which original list; the fix replaces pairwise merging with a single dependency graph built from all lists at once plus stable_topological_sort, reporting conflicts only for real cycles.

# Root cause

The responsible function is `Media.merge()` in `django/forms/widgets.py`, invoked
pairwise via `Media.__add__` each time a widget's media is combined into the
form's running total media object.

`merge()` only ever compares **two** lists at a time. When `MyForm().media` is
built, the widgets' JS lists are combined incrementally:

1. `['color-picker.js']` + `['text-editor.js']` → merged to
   `['color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js']` (no constraint between them, so
   whichever order they happened to end up in is kept).
2. That accumulated list is then merged with FancyTextWidget's
   `['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js']`.

By step 2, the "running total" list has already frozen an order between
`color-picker.js` and `text-editor.js` that came from an essentially
arbitrary pairwise merge in step 1, not from any real dependency. When this
frozen, accidental ordering is merged against FancyTextWidget's actual
ordering constraint, `merge()`'s two-list algorithm misinterprets the
artifact as a genuine conflict with `text-editor-extras.js` (because it only
looks at the two lists currently in front of it, and has lost the
information about which original list each ordering constraint came from).
This produces:
  - A bogus `MediaOrderConflictWarning` about `text-editor-extras.js` and
    `text-editor.js`, which were never in conflicting order in any single
    original list.
  - A final JS order that actually violates FancyTextWidget's real
    requirement (`text-editor.js` before `text-editor-extras.js` before
    `color-picker.js`).

The fundamental problem: **merge() combines two lists at a time and only
"remembers" relative order as a flat, linear list**, so ordering information
from earlier merges gets conflated with new lists in later merges, causing
transitive/accumulated artifacts to be reported as conflicts between
unrelated files.

# Fix

Stop doing incremental pairwise list-merging. Instead, treat every widget's
media list as a set of `(earlier_file, later_file)` ordering constraints
(edges) and build **one dependency graph from all the lists at once**
(collected as `MediaOrderConflictWarning`-worthy conflicts only when there is
an actual cycle in that combined graph, not an artifact of pairwise
reduction). Concretely:

- Gather all the media lists to be combined (not just two at a time).
- For each list, add a directed edge for each adjacent pair of items,
  expressing "this file must come before that file".
- Run a stable topological sort over the resulting graph
  (`django.utils.topological_sort.stable_topological_sort`, added for this
  fix) to produce the final ordered list.
- Only raise `MediaOrderConflictWarning` when the topological sort detects
  an actual cycle among the combined constraints (i.e., a real conflict
  between two original lists), rather than whenever two intermediate merges
  happen to disagree.

This is exactly the resolution already recorded in project memory: replace
`Media.merge()`'s pairwise merging in `django/forms/widgets.py` with a
graph-based combination of *all* input lists simultaneously followed by
`stable_topological_sort`, so a conflict is reported only for genuine cycles
and the final order (`text-editor.js, text-editor-extras.js,
color-picker.js`) correctly satisfies FancyTextWidget's real constraint.

# Answer

**Responsible function:** `Media.merge()` in `django/forms/widgets.py`, invoked pairwise by `Media.__add__` each time a widget's media is added to the running combined `Media` object.

**What is wrong:**

`Media.merge()` only ever merges *two* lists at a time. When a form has more than two widgets, `MyForm().media` is built by repeatedly calling `__add__`/`merge()` on a running "combined-so-far" list and the next widget's list, e.g.:

```
merge(merge(colorpicker_js, simpletext_js), fancytext_js)
```

The first merge produces `['color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js']` (or some order) as an intermediate list. This intermediate list is *not* one of the original declared lists — it's an artifact that mixes files from unrelated widgets that never had any real ordering relationship (`color-picker.js` and `text-editor.js` were never ordered relative to each other by any widget). When this intermediate artifact is then merged against `FancyTextWidget`'s list `['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js']`, the pairwise algorithm treats the accidental position of `color-picker.js` before `text-editor.js` in the intermediate list as if it were a real, sourced constraint, and reports a bogus conflict against `text-editor-extras.js`/`text-editor.js`, while also emitting a final order that does not respect FancyTextWidget's real constraint (text-editor.js → text-editor-extras.js → color-picker.js).

In short: pairwise merging loses provenance. By the time the third list arrives, the algorithm can no longer distinguish "these two items are ordered because one original list said so" from "these two items ended up adjacent merely because of how two previous lists were folded together." A two-at-a-time merge is not associative/transitive-safe for combining more than two order-constrained sequences, so real constraints can get corrupted and phantom conflicts appear.

**Fix:**

Don't merge two-at-a-time. Instead, collect *all* the original per-widget lists first, and build a single dependency graph (edges `a -> b` meaning "a comes before b") from every pair of adjacent elements in every original list, considered all together rather than accumulated through a chain of pairwise merges. Then perform one topological sort over that whole graph (e.g. using `django.utils.topological_sort.stable_topological_sort`) to produce the final order. A `MediaOrderConflictWarning` should then only be raised when the graph actually contains a cycle (a genuine contradiction between two original lists), not when an intermediate merge artifact happens to look like one.

This is exactly the fix applied in this repository's history (see `.neuron/learning.md`): replace `Media.merge()`'s pairwise algorithm with a graph-based approach that considers all input lists at once and topologically sorts them, only reporting conflicts on real cycles.

# Root cause and fix

**Responsible function:** `Media.merge()` in `django/forms/widgets.py`, invoked via `Media.__add__` each time widget media is combined with `+`.

**What's wrong:**
`Media.merge()` only merges *two* lists at a time. When a form has more than two widgets, their JS lists are combined pairwise, accumulating into a single "running total" list as each subsequent widget's media is added via `__add__`. By the time a third (or later) widget's list is merged in, the running merged list is just a flat list of filenames — it has lost all information about which relative orderings came from which original `Media` declaration. A later pairwise merge can then misinterpret an accidental adjacency/ordering artifact of an earlier merge as if it were a real ordering constraint from one of the original lists, and vice versa treat a genuine constraint as a conflict. This is exactly what happens with `ColorPicker`, `SimpleTextWidget`, and `FancyTextWidget`: after `ColorPicker.media + SimpleTextWidget.media` are merged first, the running list places `color-picker.js` in a position that spuriously conflicts with `FancyTextWidget`'s real requirement of `text-editor.js, text-editor-extras.js, color-picker.js`, even though no two original lists actually disagree on the order of `text-editor.js` vs `text-editor-extras.js`.

**Fix:**
Stop doing sequential/pairwise merges. Instead, collect *all* the original media lists first (e.g. via `Media.__add__` simply storing all the constituent `_js`/`_css` lists instead of eagerly merging), then build one dependency graph across **all** lists at once (an edge for each pair of directly-adjacent items within a single list), and perform a single topological sort over that combined graph to produce the final order. Using `django.utils.topological_sort.stable_topological_sort` for this, a `MediaOrderConflictWarning` is only raised when there is an actual cycle in the combined dependency graph — i.e., a genuine contradiction between the original lists — rather than an artifact introduced by merging two lists at a time and discarding the provenance of each ordering constraint.

# Where the bug is

The relevant function is `Media.merge()` (a static method) in `django/forms/widgets.py`.

It is called (indirectly, via `__add__`/`media_property`, which combines the `_js_lists`/`_css_lists`
of each widget/form pairwise with `functools.reduce(merge, lists)`) whenever the JS/CSS lists of
several widgets need to be combined into a single ordered list for a `Media` object such as
`MyForm().media`.

# What `merge()` does, and what is wrong with it

```python
@staticmethod
def merge(list_1, list_2):
    combined_list = list(list_1)
    last_insert_index = len(list_1)
    for path in reversed(list_2):
        try:
            index = combined_list.index(path)
        except ValueError:
            combined_list.insert(last_insert_index, path)
        else:
            if index > last_insert_index:
                warnings.warn(... MediaOrderConflictWarning ...)
            last_insert_index = index
    return combined_list
```

The algorithm merges only **two lists at a time**, and it walks `list_2` from the end towards the
beginning, tracking a single `last_insert_index` "pointer" into `combined_list`. Whenever an
element of `list_2` is already present in `combined_list`, it:

1. Complains if that element's index is *greater* than `last_insert_index` (i.e. it appears
   "later" than an element that, in `list_2`, comes *after* it) — even though this can happen for
   perfectly consistent orderings, and
2. Unconditionally resets `last_insert_index` to that element's index for the *rest* of the walk,
   which throws away information about the ordering constraints established so far.

Concretely, for the example in the question:

* `ColorPicker.Media.js = ['color-picker.js']`
* `SimpleTextWidget.Media.js = ['text-editor.js']`
* `FancyTextWidget.Media.js = ['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js']`

Django's form `media_property` merges each widget's media into the form's, in field-declaration
order: first `ColorPicker`'s js is merged with `SimpleTextWidget`'s js, giving
`['color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js']` (because `merge` just appends anything not seen before, it
has no reason to put `text-editor.js` before `color-picker.js` — it only saw them in two
independent single-element lists, so there was never an ordering constraint between them at that
point). Only *afterwards* is this two-element result merged with `FancyTextWidget`'s three-element
list `['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js']`.

At that point `merge(['color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js'], ['text-editor.js',
'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js'])` is called. Walking `list_2` in reverse:

1. `path = 'color-picker.js'`: found in `combined_list` at index 0. `last_insert_index` starts at
   2 (`len(list_1)`), 0 is not > 2, so no warning; `last_insert_index` becomes 0.
2. `path = 'text-editor-extras.js'`: not in `combined_list`, inserted at index 0 →
   `['text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js']`.
3. `path = 'text-editor.js'`: found in `combined_list` at index 2. Since `2 > last_insert_index`
   (0), Django wrongly warns of a `MediaOrderConflictWarning` between `text-editor-extras.js` and
   `text-editor.js` — even though `FancyTextWidget.Media.js` states unambiguously that
   `text-editor.js` must come *before* `text-editor-extras.js`, so there is no real conflict at
   all. Worse, the resulting order (`text-editor-extras.js, color-picker.js, text-editor.js` after
   the final `last_insert_index` update) actually **violates** the ordering explicitly required by
   `FancyTextWidget.Media.js`.

The root cause is that `merge()`'s single `last_insert_index` bookkeeping approach only works
correctly for lists that never require an element to be moved earlier than an element already
placed from an *unrelated*, independently-ordered fragment, and it forgets constraints as soon as
an already-seen element is encountered again — it does not build a true dependency/order graph, so
it cannot correctly reconcile three or more lists whose *pairwise* merges create false or
contradictory orderings, nor can it tell a genuine order conflict (the same two files ordered
differently in two lists) from a spurious one (files whose relative order was never actually
specified together before).

# How to fix it

Replace the "sequential index-shifting" algorithm with an approach that computes the actual
partial order implied by *all* the lists and produces a correct topological sort, e.g.:

1. Build a directed graph where, for every list being merged, each element has an edge to the
   next element in that same list (i.e., record the "X must come before Y" pairs actually stated
   in any list).
2. Perform a topological sort (e.g. depth-first search postorder, as Django's actual upstream fix
   does) over the union of all lists to produce the combined ordering, appending any items with no
   stated order relative to others in whatever stable order they first appear.
3. Only raise `MediaOrderConflictWarning` when the graph itself contains a genuine cycle (i.e. two
   elements are ordered both ways across the given lists), not merely because of the mechanics of
   how a two-list, index-based merge happens to place them.

This is essentially what Django's real fix (in later versions) does: `Media.merge` was rewritten
to build a dependency graph from consecutive pairs in each list and do a stable topological sort,
detecting true cycles/conflicts instead of relying on a single shifting insertion index that loses
context across more than two lists. That correctly yields
`['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js']` for the example above with no
spurious warning.

results.finishSummary: Media.merge in django/forms/widgets.py uses a flawed reverse-walk/last_insert_index heuristic instead of a real order-preserving (topological) merge, causing false MediaOrderConflictWarnings and incorrect ordering when combining more than two widgets' Media; the fix is to merge all lists at once via a dependency-graph based stable topological sort (only warning on genuine cycles), as detailed in ANSWER.md.

# Which function combines the media lists

`django.forms.widgets.Media.merge` (a static method on the `Media` class,
`django/forms/widgets.py`, around line 118) is responsible for combining the
JS/CSS lists of two widgets. It is called repeatedly (pairwise, via reduce)
in `media_property`/`Media.__add__`/`Widget.media` to fold together all the
widgets' `Media` declarations, e.g. for `MyForm` it ends up computing:

```
merge(merge(ColorPicker.js, SimpleTextWidget.js), FancyTextWidget.js)
```

i.e.

```
merge(merge(['color-picker.js'], ['text-editor.js']), ['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js'])
```

# What is wrong with the current algorithm

`merge(list_1, list_2)` walks `list_2` **in reverse** and, for every element
not yet in `combined_list`, inserts it right before the position
(`last_insert_index`) of the previous element it just processed. Whenever an
element from `list_2` is already present in `combined_list`, it just moves
`last_insert_index` to that element's index and does *not* actually check
whether the *relative order of that element with respect to the other
elements already merged in from list_2* is consistent — it only compares the
found `index` against the single value `last_insert_index` left over from
the *previous* iteration.

This is a purely "local", single-pointer heuristic, not a real order-aware
merge (topological sort). It only remembers "the last place I inserted
something", not "the full set of ordering constraints seen so far in
list_2". As a result:

* It can raise a `MediaOrderConflictWarning` for two elements even when they
  are *not* actually in conflicting order in the two source lists (a false
  positive) — because the comparison is against `last_insert_index`, an
  artifact of iteration order/insertion, not the genuine relative order of
  the two elements in `list_1`/`list_2`.
* Because merging is done by folding pairwise over more than two lists
  (`reduce`-like `__add__`/`media_property`), the intermediate result
  `combined_list` after merging list_1 and list_2 may already have
  reordered things in a way that breaks the ordering constraint stated by a
  *later* list (e.g. `FancyTextWidget`'s explicit
  `text-editor.js, text-editor-extras.js, color-picker.js` order), which is
  exactly what happens in the example: after merging ColorPicker's and
  SimpleTextWidget's JS (`['color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js']`), merging in
  FancyTextWidget's list moves `text-editor-extras.js` in front of
  `text-editor.js`... producing a final order that violates
  FancyTextWidget's own stated order and triggers a spurious warning about
  `text-editor.js`/`text-editor-extras.js` (which were never actually in
  conflicting order — FancyTextWidget lists them consistently as
  `text-editor.js` before `text-editor-extras.js` every time).

In short: `Media.merge`'s "walk backwards, remember only the last insertion
point" algorithm is not a correct order-preserving merge; it conflates
"element already merged in a previous list" with "element's relative
position constraint," so it both (a) reports false ordering conflicts and
(b) can produce a combined ordering that violates the real constraints
supplied by the individual lists, especially once more than two lists are
folded together pairwise.

# How to fix it

Replace the ad hoc reverse-insertion heuristic with a proper
order-preserving merge based on the actual partial order defined by *all*
the input lists — i.e. a topological sort:

1. Treat each list as a sequence of "A must come before B" constraints
   (each consecutive pair in each list is an edge in a directed graph).
2. Build a dependency graph over all files mentioned across every widget's
   Media list (not just pairwise reduce of two lists at a time — collect
   all the lists for the same media type before merging, then merge them
   all at once).
3. Perform a stable topological sort of that graph (preserving the
   original relative order among elements when there is no explicit
   constraint between them, and only emitting a `MediaOrderConflictWarning`
   when the graph actually contains a genuine cycle, i.e. some pair of
   elements is ordered oppositely in two different lists).

This is essentially the approach Django's later fix for this exact bug
(ticket #30748) took: `Media.merge` was rewritten to combine *all* the
media lists at once (not fold two-at-a-time) and to detect true conflicts
by checking whether the same two elements appear in opposite relative order
in two different lists, rather than relying on the single
`last_insert_index` pointer from a single backward pass. Concretely:

```python
@staticmethod
def merge(*lists):
    """
    Merge lists while trying to keep the relative order of the elements.
    Warn if the lists have the same two elements in a different relative
    order.
    """
    dependency_graph = defaultdict(set)
    all_items = OrderedSet()
    for list_ in filter(None, lists):
        head = list_[0]
        # The first items depend on nothing but have to be part of the
        # dependency graph to be included in the result.
        dependency_graph.setdefault(head, set())
        for item in list_:
            all_items.add(item)
        for head, item in zip(list_, list_[1:]):
            dependency_graph[item].add(head)
    try:
        return stable_topological_sort(all_items, dependency_graph)
    except CyclicDependencyError:
        warnings.warn(
            'Detected duplicate Media files in an opposite order: {}'.format(
                ', '.join(repr(l) for l in lists)
            ),
            MediaOrderConflictWarning,
        )
        return list(all_items)
```

with a helper such as:

```python
def stable_topological_sort(nodes, dependency_graph):
    result = []
    for node in nodes:
        _insert(node, dependency_graph, result, set())
    return result
```

using Kahn's algorithm / DFS-based topological sort with cycle detection.
Applying this to the example correctly merges the three widgets' JS media
into `['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js']`
(the order dictated by `FancyTextWidget`, which is consistent with the
other two widgets), with no warning, because there is genuinely no cyclic
ordering constraint among the three files.

# Answer

## Responsible function

`django.forms.widgets.Media.merge` (a static method on the `Media` class in `django/forms/widgets.py`, around line 118). This is the function that is repeatedly called (via `Media.__add__`/`__radd__`, invoked when combining widget `Media` objects on a form) to pairwise-combine the `js`/`css` lists of the different widgets' `Media` classes.

## What is wrong

`merge(list_1, list_2)` implements a naive "two-list merge" heuristic: it starts with a copy of `list_1`, then walks `list_2` **in reverse**, and for each element either inserts it right before the last successfully-matched position, or — if the element is already present in `combined_list` — checks whether its index is *after* the current `last_insert_index`. If so it emits a `MediaOrderConflictWarning`, and then unconditionally moves `last_insert_index` to that element's position.

The problem is that this algorithm only ever compares each list against the running merged result using a single "cursor" (`last_insert_index`), rather than doing a true, transitive ordering/topological sort of *all* the pairwise adjacency constraints implied by each individual list. It effectively treats the two lists as if only adjacent-order relationships need to be preserved, and it decides "conflict" purely based on where an item currently sits in the partially-built `combined_list`, which depends on the arbitrary order in which merges happen to be performed (form field iteration order), not on the real content of the constraints.

Concretely, with:
- `background_color` (ColorPicker): `['color-picker.js']`
- `intro` (SimpleTextWidget): `['text-editor.js']`
- `body` (FancyTextWidget): `['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js']`

Django's `Media.merge` is called pairwise in field order. First it merges ColorPicker's `['color-picker.js']` with SimpleTextWidget's `['text-editor.js']`, giving e.g. `['color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js']` (no real relationship between them, so either order is "valid" from that merge's point of view). Only *then* is this combined list merged with FancyTextWidget's list `['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js']`.

When merging `['color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js']` (list_1) with `['text-editor-extras.js', ...]`/FancyTextWidget's list (list_2), the algorithm never sees FancyTextWidget's list as a single ordering fact "text-editor.js < text-editor-extras.js < color-picker.js" — it only compares elements one at a time against the *already fixed* position of `color-picker.js` (which was accidentally placed *before* `text-editor.js` in the first pairwise merge, an ordering nobody actually required). Because `color-picker.js` ends up before `text-editor.js` in `combined_list`, but FancyTextWidget requires `text-editor.js` before `color-picker.js`, `merge` thinks `text-editor.js`/`text-editor-extras.js` (or `color-picker.js`) are in "conflicting order" and raises `MediaOrderConflictWarning` — even though `text-editor.js`, `text-editor-extras.js`, and `color-picker.js` are listed in the *same* relative order in every single Media declaration that mentions them (only inside FancyTextWidget). There is no genuine conflict at all; the algorithm is fooled by an accidental, unconstrained ordering decision it made in an earlier, unrelated pairwise merge, and it also produces a final order that violates FancyTextWidget's own required order (color-picker.js can end up before text-editor.js/text-editor-extras.js).

In short: **the bug is that `Media.merge`'s incremental, single-cursor list-splicing algorithm does not correctly perform a topological sort over the union of ordering constraints from all the media lists; it conflates "no stated relationship yet" with "must come before", and lets accidental orderings introduced by earlier, unrelated merges create spurious conflicts and violate real constraints from later merges.**

## How to fix it

Replace the ad-hoc pairwise splice algorithm with a proper topological sort:

1. Treat each input list as a sequence of ordering constraints (`a` appears before `b` for every consecutive/ordered pair `a, b` within that single list only — i.e., build a dependency graph from each list, not from the partially-built combined result).
2. Collect all such "before" edges from **all** the lists being merged (this generalizes better than pairwise `functools.reduce(merge, ...)` — ideally `Media.merge` should be given all the lists at once, or repeated pairwise merges should build/update an explicit graph rather than mutating a flat list positionally).
3. Perform a stable topological sort (e.g. using Kahn's algorithm, preserving original relative/insertion order among items with no explicit constraint between them) over this graph to produce the final ordered list.
4. Only raise `MediaOrderConflictWarning` when the constraint graph actually contains a cycle (i.e., some pair of files is truly required to be in opposite order by two different declarations) — not just because of the incidental position an element happens to hold in a previous partial merge result.

This is essentially the fix Django itself later applied (Django's `Media.merge` was rewritten, in response to this exact bug — ticket #30498, fixed in Django 3.1 — to perform a stable topological sort using a "dependency graph" approach based on `MediaOrderConflictWarning` being raised only for genuine cycles), so that combining `ColorPicker`, `SimpleTextWidget`, and `FancyTextWidget`'s media correctly yields `text-editor.js, text-editor-extras.js, color-picker.js` with no spurious warning.

results.finishSummary: The bug is in Media.merge() in django/forms/widgets.py, which uses a naive reverse-order, index-splice insertion heuristic instead of a real topological sort over the ordering constraints implied by all lists, causing false conflict warnings and an invalid merged order; the fix is to build a precedence graph from consecutive pairs in each list and topologically sort it, only warning on genuine cycles.
results.answerText:
# Media merge order bug

## Where

`django/forms/widgets.py`, the `Media.merge()` static method (used by
`Media.__add__`/the `+` operator that `Media._css`/`Media._js` combination
relies on, and ultimately by `Form.media`, which successively adds each
field/widget's `Media` object together).

## What's wrong

`merge(list_1, list_2)` is a heuristic, pairwise, single-pass "merge by
insertion" algorithm, not a real topological sort. It:

1. Starts from a copy of `list_1`.
2. Walks `list_2` **in reverse**, and for each item either inserts it at
   `last_insert_index` (if not already present) or, if it is already
   present, moves `last_insert_index` to that item's index and only checks
   whether that single item is now "out of order" relative to the
   *previous* single item it looked at.

Because it only ever compares the current item to the last item it
processed (tracked via `last_insert_index`) — not to the full set of
ordering constraints implied by every list involved — it can:

* Falsely report a conflict between two elements that never actually
  appear in opposite relative order in any input list (as with
  `text-editor.js` / `text-editor-extras.js` in `FancyTextWidget.Media`,
  which lists them in the same order every time they occur).
* Produce a final combined order that violates a real ordering
  constraint from one of the input lists (i.e., the merge isn't
  guaranteed to respect all pairwise "A must come before B" constraints
  simultaneously), because as soon as `last_insert_index` is updated for
  one match, earlier/later relationships from the *same* list can end up
  scrambled once a third, independent list is merged in.

In short: `Media.merge` treats "merging two lists" as a local,
index-based splice operation instead of building a full precedence graph
of "X must come before Y" edges (deduced from adjacent-pair ordering in
each input list) and then deriving a valid total order (topological
sort) that satisfies all of them. Doing pairwise merges of more than two
lists (as happens when a `Form` combines the `Media` of many widgets,
each merge feeding into the next) compounds this, because each 2-list
merge can silently discard/contradict ordering information established
by a previous merge.

Concretely, for this example:

* `ColorPicker.Media.js = ['color-picker.js']`
* `SimpleTextWidget.Media.js = ['text-editor.js']`
* `FancyTextWidget.Media.js = ['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js']`

When Django merges these three lists pairwise with `merge()`, the
insertion-based algorithm ends up comparing `text-editor-extras.js`
against `text-editor.js` using stale `last_insert_index` bookkeping left
over from merging in `color-picker.js`, and reports them as being in
conflicting order even though `FancyTextWidget` lists them consistently
as `text-editor.js` before `text-editor-extras.js` every time. The
resulting combined list also does not preserve
`text-editor.js, text-editor-extras.js, color-picker.js`.

## How to fix it

Replace the ad hoc insertion algorithm with a proper dependency-graph /
topological-sort based merge:

1. Build a directed graph of "must precede" edges by looking, in each
   input list to merge, at every consecutive pair `(a, b)` and adding an
   edge `a -> b` (meaning "a must come before b").
2. Union all elements from both lists as graph nodes.
3. Perform a stable topological sort over that graph (e.g. Kahn's
   algorithm, preferring to keep elements in their original relative
   order among ties, similar to what CPython's `graphlib.TopologicalSorter`
   or a manual DFS-based topo-sort would give).
4. Only raise `MediaOrderConflictWarning` when the graph actually has a
   cycle (i.e., there exist elements `a` and `b` such that both `a -> b`
   and `b -> a` are implied by the combined edge set) — not merely
   because of incidental index positions during a single linear pass.

This is essentially the actual fix Django later shipped upstream: `Media.merge`
was rewritten to build a dependency graph from consecutive pairs across all
lists being combined and compute a topological order from it (raising the
conflict warning only for genuine cycles), rather than doing a single
reverse-order, index-based list splice. With such an approach, merging
`['color-picker.js']`, `['text-editor.js']`, and
`['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js']` yields the
edges `text-editor.js -> text-editor-extras.js` and
`text-editor-extras.js -> color-picker.js` with no cycle, and the sort
correctly produces `text-editor.js, text-editor-extras.js, color-picker.js`
without any spurious warning.
